content: The primary outcomes of interest in the treatment of multidrug-resistant and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) include treatment success, failure and recurrence, mortality, loss to follow-up, adverse events, and the amplification of drug resistance. These outcomes are evaluated in both inpatient and outpatient settings, with a focus on public health and health systems perspectives. MDR/RR-TB has become a significant global health challenge due to inadequate management of drug-susceptible tuberculosis and the transmission of drug-resistant strains. While MDR/RR-TB is treatable, it requires specialized treatment regimens that are often longer and involve potentially more toxic medications. Efforts to reduce the duration of treatment have driven the search for shorter and safer regimens. In 2016, based on observational studies conducted in Asia and Africa, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended a standardized 9-month treatment regimen for eligible patients. This regimen included an injectable agent and was shorter than the standard 18–20 months of care. In 2018, following the results of the STREAM Stage 1 trial, modifications were made to this regimen, including replacing kanamycin with amikacin due to evidence of better comparative effectiveness. However, concerns about the permanent toxic effects of injectable agents have led to the development of shorter, injectable-sparing regimens. South Africa provided observational data to WHO on a 9-month all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline, which was reviewed and recommended by WHO in 2019. This regimen included a combination of medicines such as bedaquiline, levofloxacin (or moxifloxacin), ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, and clofazimine. In 2022, new evidence from South Africa led to a modification of this regimen, replacing 4 months of ethionamide with 2 months of linezolid (600 mg). The Nix-TB study, conducted by the Global TB Alliance, evaluated a novel 6-month regimen consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid. This regimen was assessed for its safety and effectiveness in improving treatment outcomes for patients with MDR/RR-TB and additional resistance to fluoroquinolones. However, limitations in study design, small sample sizes, and observed adverse events prevented the WHO panel from recommending global programmatic implementation of this regimen until further evidence is available. In 2020, WHO guidelines recommended the use of the BPaL regimen under operational research conditions. Two randomized controlled trials, TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix, concluded in 2021, providing new evidence for WHO to assess and update recommendations for MDR/RR-TB treatment. The TB-PRACTECAL trial compared the BPaLM regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin) to the BPaL regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid). The panel judged the benefits of BPaLM to be moderate and the undesirable effects to be small, though the certainty of evidence was very low. The balance of health effects likely favors the BPaLM regimen. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly disrupted TB services, reversing years of progress. There was an 18% global decline in the number of newly diagnosed TB cases in 2020 compared to 2019, with a corresponding increase in TB-related deaths. Access to treatment for drug-resistant TB also declined by 15%, with only about one-third of those in need receiving treatment. Despite these challenges, treatment success rates for MDR/RR-TB have improved globally, reaching 59% in 2018 compared to 50% in 2012. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of shorter, safer, and more effective regimens for MDR/RR-TB. The BPaLM regimen is recommended for patients with MDR/RR-TB, with or without fluoroquinolone resistance, who have not been previously exposed to bedaquiline and linezolid or have been exposed for less than one month. However, the implementation of these regimens may face challenges, including the need for drug susceptibility testing (DST) and drug safety monitoring, particularly in resource-limited settings. The panel judged the BPaLM regimen to be probably acceptable and feasible for implementation, though barriers such as limited access to rapid DST for moxifloxacin remain. In conclusion, the WHO strongly recommends the use of the 6-month BPaLM regimen for MDR/RR-TB patients, based on its potential to improve treatment outcomes while reducing treatment duration and toxicity.
